idiom_name: Mutex#synchronize boundary + private helpers (Monitor as the reentrant escape)
implementation_notes: Ruby's Mutex is not reentrant and says so loudly: a second lock by the owning thread raises ThreadError ('deadlock; recursive locking') instead of hanging, so an intra-component call that re-locks fails fast and the interface/implementation split is the standard answer - public methods wrap their body in @mutex.synchronize (which releases on exceptions and on return) and private helpers assume the lock is held. Monitor is the library-provided reentrant alternative: enter/exit keep a count and an owner, so nested synchronize blocks work, which is convenient for components that must re-enter but hides exactly the extra acquisition the pattern exists to expose. Thread::Queue's blocking pop is the idiomatic replacement when the guarded state can be owned by a single consumer; note that under the GVL only the mutex protects multi-step invariants, and that Ractors do not share ordinary objects at all.
pitfalls: Mutex#lock raises ThreadError on recursive locking, but only for the same thread - a nested call reached through a different thread still blocks, so the split is mandatory regardless.
The GVL does not make compound operations atomic (a thread can switch between bytecodes) and Ractors do not share mutable objects, so cross-Ractor state needs explicit messaging rather than a lock.
Monitor (reentrant) removes the error signal Mutex gives you: nested synchronize silently succeeds and the hold count grows.
A private helper is a convention only - Object#send and mixins can reach it - and a helper that calls a public method re-enters the mutex.
